{"type":"item.completed","item":{"id":"item_1","type":"command_execution","command":"/bin/bash -lc \"sed -n '1,260p' /tests/instruction_reference.md\"","aggregated_output":"# Training a Neural Decoder\n\n---\n\n## ⚠️ CRITICAL CONSTRAINTS — READ FIRST ⚠️\n\n**Before doing ANYTHING else, read and internalize these rules:**\n\n1. **CREATE CONVERSION_NOTES.md IMMEDIATELY**: Your very first action must be to create `CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. Do this BEFORE exploring any code or data. Document everything in this file as you work.\n\n2. **FOLLOW STEPS IN ORDER**: Do not skip steps. Do not proceed to step N+1 until step N is complete. Each step has \"Done when\" criteria — verify them before moving on.\n\n3. **MATCH THE REFERENCE PROCESSING**: Your processing must match what's described in the reference paper and code. You will be assessed on this consistency.\n\n---\n\n## Project Context\n\n- You are a computational neuroscientist. Your goal is to load and reformat data from a neuroscience paper into a specified structure suitable for downstream analysis.\n- You need to use the **SAME** processing of the data described in the provided reference paper and code repository. \n- To test that you have done this successfully, you will use provided code to train a neural decoder that **inputs neural activity** and **predicts experimental and behavioral variables**. \n- We will assess your correctness on **matching the loading and processing described in the reference texts and code**. \n\n## Reference Information\n\n- The reference **paper** \"Unsupervised pretraining in biological neural networks\" is in the file `paper.pdf`.\n- Some parts of the paper that describe the experiment and processing have been copied to the file `methods.txt`. \n- **Code** from the paper are in the directory `code`.\n- **Data** from the paper are in the directory `data`.\n\n## Decoder Task\n\nTemporally aligned based on trial start (corridor entry).\n\n### Decoder Inputs:\n- Time to sound cue, continuous, time-varying\n- Day of training, continuous, per-trial\n- Time since trial start, continuous, time varying\n- Reward availability: 1 if in rewarded corridor, 0 if not, discrete, per-trial\n\n### Decoder Outputs\n- Visual stimulus category. e.g. circle1, leaf2, etc., per-trial\n- Licking, binary, time-varying. 0 = not licking, 1 = licking\n- Position in corridor discretized into 4 equal-length, 1-m-long spatial bins, time varying\n- Running speed discretized into 4 bins, each corresponding to 25% of the data\n\n## Target Data Format\n\n- Save the full converted dataset to the pickle file `converted_data.pkl`.\n- All datasets must be converted into the following Python dictionary structure:\n\n```python\ndata = {\n    'neural': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # shape: (n_neurons, n_timepoints)\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # trial 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        [  # list of trials for session 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'input': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            input_data,  # stimulus/task variables, shape: (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'output': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'subjects': list of str, # ids of all subjects, length n_subjects\n    'subject_idx': shape (n_sessions,), # index into subjects for each session\n\n    'brain_regions': list of str, # names of the brain regions recorded from, e.g. ALM, V1\n    'brain_region_idx': [ # list of sessions\n        neuron_region_idx, # shape: (n_neurons,)\n    ] # index into `brain_regions` for each neuron\n\n    'input_names': list of str, # names for each input, of length n_input\n    'output_names': list of str, # names of each output, of length n_output\n    'output_values': [ # list of length n_output\n        [ output_val0, ... ], # list of str of length d_output[0], name of each output value\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'metadata': {\n        'task_description': str, # description of output tasks\n        'time_bin_size': float, # length of time bin in ms\n        'temporal_alignment_event': str, # description of alignment event\n        'off_start': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to start of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        'off_end': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to end of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        ...\n    }\n}\n```\n\n### Key Format Requirements\n\n- **neural**: Neural activity data (e.g., firing rates, spike counts) organized by session and trial\n  - Dimensions: (n_neurons, n_timepoints) for each trial.\n  - Time bins should be the same size for all trials and sessions. \n  - There needs to be at least two trials within each session in order to evaluate the decoder performance.\n\n- **input**: Variables that serve as inputs **to the decoder**\n  - These are **decoder inputs**. They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\n  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \n  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\n  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\n  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\n- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\n  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\n\n- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\n- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\n\n- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\n  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \n\n- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\n  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\n- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\n  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\n\n- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \n  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\n  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\n  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \n  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\n  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\n\n## Python environment\n\n- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\n- Use `python3` to run any python code.\n- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\n\n## Decoder Reference\n\n- Run this script with `python train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\n- Optional arguments:\n  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\n  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\n  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\n- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\n\n### Purpose\n\nThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\n1. Data structure is correct - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n2. Dimensions are consistent - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n3. Values are sensible - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n4. Decoder can successfully train and predict\n5. Poor performance indicates data formatting issues that need investigation\n\n### Consistency requirements\n\nYour processing and formatting must **match the reference paper and code** with respect to:\n- Loading of data\n- Temporal alignment of different time series streams (neural, inputs, outputs)\n- Processing of neural, input, and output data streams\n- Curation of data: filtering of low-quality neurons, trials, sessions, and mice.\n\nTo check consistency, you must compare statistics available in the reference paper and your converted dataset. \n\nWhenever possible, invent **SANITY CHECKS** that your loading and processing matches the reference paper and code. \n\nDiscrepancies are only allowed if required by the Decoder Input and Decoder Output specifications above. \n\nCarefully verify your work after every step. When you find mistakes, document and fix them immediately. Be critical of results **after every step of processing**. \n\nYou will be assessed on whether the decisions you make on how to load, filter, process, align, reformat, and save the data are reasonable and match the reference paper and code and these instructions. During testing, the reference version of `train_decoder.py` will be run on your converted data. Data statistics and decoder accuracy will be compared to those achieved by human-written conversion code. \n\n---\n\n## Conversion Workflow\n\n**IMPORTANT**: Follow these steps in order. Each step has explicit completion criteria. Do not proceed to the next step until the current step is complete. Use the exact step names below when documenting progress in CONVERSION_NOTES.md.\n\n**STATUS TRACKING**: At the start of each step, update its status to `IN PROGRESS` in CONVERSION_NOTES.md. When complete, update to `COMPLETE`. This helps you and the user track progress.\n\n---\n\n### Step 0: Setup and Initialization\n\n**Goal**: Set up the working environment and create the notes file.\n\n**Actions**:\n1. **FIRST**: Create `CONVERSION_NOTES.md` with the template structure shown at the end of this document\n2. Verify you can run `python3` and import key packages (numpy, torch)\n3. List the contents of this directory to understand what files are available\n4. **REMINDER**: Do NOT look at any files outside this directory\n\n**Done when**: \n- `CONVERSION_NOTES.md` exists with the proper template structure\n- You have confirmed Python and key packages work\n- You have listed directory contents in CONVERSION_NOTES.md\n\n**⚠️ CHECKPOINT**: Before proceeding to Step 1, verify that `CONVERSION_NOTES.md` exists by running `ls -la CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. If it doesn't exist, STOP and create it now.\n\n---\n\n### Step 1: Reference Code Exploration\n\n**⚠️ CONSTRAINT REMINDER**: Only look at code in the `code` directory. Do NOT look outside this project directory.\n\n**Goal**: Understand how the original authors loaded and processed their data.\n\n**Actions**:\n- Look for documentation or README files in the `code` directory\n- Read the provided reference code bases to see how the reference paper loaded and manipulated the data\n- Understand which functions are being called to read, curate, process, and manipulate the data\n- For neural imaging data, does delta F over F need to be computed? \n- For electrophysiology neural data, do cells need to be filtered based on quality? \n- Note to file important functions, their inputs, and outputs\n\n**Done when**: You have documented key functions and their purposes in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \"Step 1\".\n\n**⚠️ CHECKPOINT**: Before proceeding to Step 2, update Step 1 CONVERSION_NOTES.md.\n\n---\n\n### Step 2: Dataset Exploration\n\n**⚠️ CONSTRAINT REMINDER**: Only look at data in the `data` directory. Do NOT look outside this project directory.\n\n**Goal**: Understand the native data structure\n\n**Actions**:\n- Identify how data is organized (all files, formats, hierarchies)\n- Determine available variables and their meanings\n- Check data dimensions and data types\n- Look for documentation or README files\n- Note the data organization and structure\n- Note dataset size parameters such as the **total number** of subjects (mice), sessions, trials, and neurons\n\n**Done when**: You have documented the data structure, file formats, size, and available variables in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \"Step 2\".\n\n","exit_code":0,"status":"completed"}}

{"type":"item.completed","item":{"id":"item_3","type":"command_execution","command":"/bin/bash -lc \"sed -n '1,320p' /app/convert_data.py\"","aggregated_output":"#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\"\"\"\nConvert Zhong et al. 2025 data to decoder-compatible format.\n\nUsage:\n    python -u convert_data.py <outpicklefile> [--full|--sample] [--show-processing]\n\nThe data consists of 2-photon calcium imaging recordings from mouse visual cortex\nduring a VR corridor navigation task. Mice ran through corridors with different\nvisual textures and received water rewards in one corridor type.\n\"\"\"\n\nimport os\nimport sys\nimport time\nimport argparse\nimport pickle\nimport numpy as np\nfrom collections import defaultdict\nimport gc\nimport warnings\nwarnings.filterwarnings('ignore')\n\n# =============================================================================\n# Constants and configuration\n# =============================================================================\nDATA_ROOT = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), 'data')\nCODE_ROOT = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), 'code')\n\n# Brain region mapping from iarea values (from utils.py: neu_area_ID)\nAREA_MAP = {\n    8: 'V1',\n    0: 'mHV', 1: 'mHV', 2: 'mHV', 9: 'mHV',\n    5: 'lHV', 6: 'lHV',\n    3: 'aHV', 4: 'aHV',\n    -1: 'other', 7: 'other',\n}\n\nBRAIN_REGIONS = ['V1', 'mHV', 'lHV', 'aHV', 'other']\n\n# Position binning: 4 bins of 1m (10 dm) each over [0, 40) dm corridor\n# Gray space (40-60 dm) goes to last bin\nPOS_BIN_EDGES = [0, 10, 20, 30, 60.01]  # last bin includes gray space\nPOS_BIN_LABELS = ['0-1m', '1-2m', '2-3m', '3m+']\n\n# =============================================================================\n# Data loading functions (adapted from reference code utils.py)\n# =============================================================================\n\ndef load_spk(db):\n    \"\"\"Load neural data and concatenate planes. Returns (n_neurons, n_frames).\"\"\"\n    fn = '%s_%s_%s_neural_data.npy' % (db['mname'], db['datexp'], db['blk'])\n    spk_path = os.path.join(DATA_ROOT, 'spk', fn)\n    spk = np.concatenate(\n        [nspk for nspk in np.load(spk_path, allow_pickle=True).item()['spks']], 0\n    )\n    return spk\n\n\ndef load_retino(db):\n    \"\"\"Load retinotopy data. Returns iarea array.\"\"\"\n    fn = '%s_%s_trans.npz' % (db['mname'], db['datexp'])\n    dtrans = np.load(os.path.join(DATA_ROOT, 'retinotopy', fn), allow_pickle=True)\n    return dtrans['iarea']\n\n\ndef load_beh(exp_type):\n    \"\"\"Load behavior data for an experiment type.\"\"\"\n    fn = os.path.join(DATA_ROOT, 'beh', 'Beh_%s.npy' % exp_type)\n    return np.load(fn, allow_pickle=True).item()\n\n\ndef get_beh_key(db):\n    \"\"\"Get the behavior dictionary key for a session.\"\"\"\n    if 'stimtype' in db and db['stimtype']:\n        return '%s_%s_%s_%s' % (db['mname'], db['datexp'], db['blk'], db['stimtype'])\n    return '%s_%s_%s' % (db['mname'], db['datexp'], db['blk'])\n\n\n# =============================================================================\n# Build session list\n# =============================================================================\n\ndef build_session_list():\n    \"\"\"Build list of unique sessions with their metadata.\n\n    Returns list of dicts with keys: mname, datexp, blk, exp_type, db_entry, beh_key\n    \"\"\"\n    exp_info = np.load(\n        os.path.join(DATA_ROOT, 'beh', 'Imaging_Exp_info.npy'), allow_pickle=True\n    ).item()\n\n    seen = set()\n    sessions = []\n\n    for exp_type in exp_info:\n        for db in exp_info[exp_type]:\n            key = (db['mname'], db['datexp'], db['blk'])\n            if key in seen:\n                continue\n            seen.add(key)\n\n            beh_key = get_beh_key(db)\n            sessions.append({\n                'mname': db['mname'],\n                'datexp': db['datexp'],\n                'blk': db['blk'],\n                'exp_type': exp_type,\n                'db_entry': db,\n                'beh_key': beh_key,\n                'session_key': key,\n            })\n\n    # Sort by mouse name, then date\n    sessions.sort(key=lambda s: (s['mname'], s['datexp']))\n    return sessions\n\n\ndef compute_training_days(sessions):\n    \"\"\"Compute ordinal training day for each session within each mouse.\"\"\"\n    mouse_sessions = defaultdict(list)\n    for i, s in enumerate(sessions):\n        mouse_sessions[s['mname']].append((s['datexp'], i))\n\n    days = np.zeros(len(sessions), dtype=np.float32)\n    for mname, sess_list in mouse_sessions.items():\n        sess_list.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])  # sort by date\n        for day_idx, (datexp, global_idx) in enumerate(sess_list):\n            days[global_idx] = float(day_idx)\n\n    return days\n\n\n# =============================================================================\n# Processing functions\n# =============================================================================\n\ndef compute_speed_quartiles(sessions, beh_cache):\n    \"\"\"Compute global speed quartiles across all sessions.\"\"\"\n    print(\"Computing global speed quartiles...\")\n    all_speeds = []\n    for s in sessions:\n        beh = beh_cache[s['exp_type']][s['beh_key']]\n        speeds = beh['ft_RunSpeed']\n        all_speeds.append(speeds)\n\n    all_speeds = np.concatenate(all_speeds)\n    quartiles = np.percentile(all_speeds, [25, 50, 75])\n    print(f\"  Speed quartiles: {quartiles}\")\n    print(f\"  Speed range: [{all_speeds.min():.1f}, {all_speeds.max():.1f}]\")\n    return quartiles\n\n\ndef get_all_stimuli(sessions, beh_cache):\n    \"\"\"Get sorted list of all unique stimulus names.\"\"\"\n    all_stim = set()\n    for s in sessions:\n        beh = beh_cache[s['exp_type']][s['beh_key']]\n        for wn in beh['UniqWalls']:\n            all_stim.add(str(wn))\n    return sorted(all_stim)\n\n\ndef digitize_position(pos):\n    \"\"\"Discretize position into 4 bins of 1m (10dm) each.\n    Bins: [0,10), [10,20), [20,30), [30,60+)\n    \"\"\"\n    bins = np.digitize(pos, [10, 20, 30])\n    return bins.astype(np.int64)\n\n\ndef digitize_speed(speed, quartiles):\n    \"\"\"Discretize running speed into 4 quartile bins.\"\"\"\n    bins = np.digitize(speed, quartiles)\n    return bins.astype(np.int64)\n\n\ndef make_lick_vector(beh, start_fr, end_fr):\n    \"\"\"Create binary lick vector for frames [start_fr, end_fr).\n\n    LickFr values are fractional frame indices.\n    \"\"\"\n    n_frames = end_fr - start_fr\n    lick_vec = np.zeros(n_frames, dtype=np.int64)\n\n    lick_frs = beh['LickFr']\n    # Round to nearest integer frame\n    lick_frs_int = np.round(lick_frs).astype(int)\n    # Filter to frames within this trial\n    mask = (lick_frs_int >= start_fr) & (lick_frs_int < end_fr)\n    if mask.any():\n        trial_lick_frs = lick_frs_int[mask] - start_fr\n        # Clip to valid range\n        trial_lick_frs = np.clip(trial_lick_frs, 0, n_frames - 1)\n        lick_vec[trial_lick_frs] = 1\n\n    return lick_vec\n\n\ndef get_brain_region_idx(iarea):\n    \"\"\"Map iarea values to brain_region indices.\n\n    BRAIN_REGIONS = ['V1', 'mHV', 'lHV', 'aHV', 'other']\n    \"\"\"\n    region_to_idx = {r: i for i, r in enumerate(BRAIN_REGIONS)}\n    # Vectorized mapping\n    idx = np.full(len(iarea), region_to_idx['other'], dtype=np.int64)\n    for area_val, region_name in AREA_MAP.items():\n        mask = iarea == area_val\n        idx[mask] = region_to_idx[region_name]\n    return idx\n\n\ndef process_session(session, beh, training_day, speed_quartiles, stim_to_idx, frame_period):\n    \"\"\"Process a single session into decoder format.\n\n    Returns:\n        neural_trials: list of (n_neurons, n_timepoints) arrays\n        input_trials: list of (4, n_timepoints) arrays\n        output_trials: list of (4, n_timepoints) arrays\n        brain_region_idx: (n_neurons,) array\n    \"\"\"\n    t0 = time.time()\n\n    # Load neural data\n    spk = load_spk(session['db_entry'])\n    n_neurons, n_total_frames = spk.shape\n\n    # Load retinotopy\n    iarea = load_retino(session['db_entry'])\n    brain_reg_idx = get_brain_region_idx(iarea)\n\n    # Verify consistency\n    assert len(iarea) == n_neurons, \\\n        f\"Neuron count mismatch: spk={n_neurons}, retinotopy={len(iarea)}\"\n\n    ntrials = beh['ntrials']\n    StartFr = beh['StartFr'].astype(int)\n    EndFr = beh['EndFr'].astype(int)\n    SoundFr = beh['SoundFr']\n    WallName = beh['WallName']\n    isRew = beh['isRew']\n    ft_Pos = beh['ft_Pos']\n    ft_RunSpeed = beh['ft_RunSpeed']\n\n    neural_trials = []\n    input_trials = []\n    output_trials = []\n\n    skipped = 0\n    for t in range(ntrials):\n        start = StartFr[t]\n        end = EndFr[t]\n\n        # Skip if frames out of bounds\n        if start < 0 or end > n_total_frames or end <= start:\n            skipped += 1\n            continue\n\n        # Also clip end to available frames in beh arrays\n        end = min(end, len(ft_Pos), len(ft_RunSpeed))\n        if end <= start:\n            skipped += 1\n            continue\n\n        n_tp = end - start\n        if n_tp < 2:\n            skipped += 1\n            continue\n\n        # --- Neural ---\n        neural = spk[:, start:end].astype(np.float16)\n        # Using float16 to reduce memory (decoder uses PCA, so precision is fine)\n\n        # --- Inputs ---\n        # 1. Time to sound cue (seconds): positive = time until cue, negative = time since cue\n        sound_fr = SoundFr[t]\n        frame_indices = np.arange(start, end, dtype=np.float64)\n        time_to_sound = (sound_fr - frame_indices) * frame_period  # positive before, negative after\n\n        # 2. Day of training (constant for trial)\n        day = np.full(n_tp, training_day, dtype=np.float32)\n\n        # 3. Time since trial start (seconds)\n        time_since_start = (frame_indices - start) * frame_period\n\n        # 4. Reward availability\n        rew = np.full(n_tp, float(isRew[t]), dtype=np.float32)\n\n        inp = np.stack([time_to_sound, day, time_since_start, rew], axis=0).astype(np.float32)\n\n        # --- Outputs ---\n        # 1. Visual stimulus category (per-trial, broadcast)\n        stim_name = str(WallName[t])\n        stim_idx = stim_to_idx[stim_name]\n        stim_out = np.full(n_tp, stim_idx, dtype=np.int64)\n\n        # 2. Licking (binary, time-varying)\n        lick = make_lick_vector(beh, start, end)\n\n        # 3. Position (4 bins, time-varying)\n        pos = ft_Pos[start:end]\n        pos_bin = digitize_position(pos)\n\n        # 4. Running speed (4 bins, time-varying)\n        speed = ft_RunSpeed[start:end]\n        speed_bin = digitize_speed(speed, speed_quartiles)\n\n        out = np.stack([stim_out, lick, pos_bin, speed_bin], axis=0).astype(np.int64)\n\n        neural_trials.append(neural)\n        input_trials.append(inp)\n        output_trials.append(out)\n\n    elapsed = time.time() - t0\n    if skipped > 0:\n        print(f\"    Skipped {skipped}/{ntrials} trials\")\n\n    return neural_trials, input_trials, output_trials, brain_reg_idx, elapsed\n\n","exit_code":0,"status":"completed"}}

started**: 2026-03-24\n- **Goal**: Convert to decoder-compatible format\n\n## Step 0: Setup and Initialization\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\nDirectory contents:\n- `code/` - Reference code: utils.py, for an experiment type |\n| `neu_area_ID(iarea)` | utils.py | PROCESSING | Map iarea values to brain regions: V1(8), mHV(0,1,2,9), lHV(5,6), aHV(3,4) |\n| `get_interpPos_spk()` | utils.py | PROCESSING | Interpolate neural activity into (neurons, trials, 60 position bins) |\n| `spk_pos_interp()` | utils.py | PROCESSING | Core interpolation: raw spk + cumulative pos -> trial x position matrix |\n| `dprime()` | utils.py | PROCESSING | Compute d-prime for stimulus selectivity |\n| `lickCount()` | utils.py | PROCESSING | Binary lick response per trial (before/after reward) |\n| `get_cat_id()` | utils.py | PROCESSING | Get stimulus category IDs from wall names and reward info |\n| `Get_dprime_selective_neuron()` | utils.py | CURATION | Select stimulus-selective neurons using d-prime, filter by corridor activity |\n| `Get_coding_direction()` | utils.py | PROCESSING | Coding direction analysis with normalization and cross-validation |\n\n### Key Data Flow\n1. **Neural data**: Loaded via `load_spk()` -> concatenates multiple planes of Suite2p output -> shape (n_neurons, n_frames)\n2. **Behavior**: Loaded from `Beh_{exp_type}.npy` -> dictionary with per-session behavior data\n3. **Retinotopy**: Maps neurons to visual cortex areas (V1, mHV, lHV, aHV) via `iarea` values\n4. **Processing**: Reference code primarily uses position-interpolated data (60 bins per trial) for analyses. The raw data is at ~3.17 Hz frame rate.\n5. **Neuron filtering in reference**: Corridor-active neurons selected (higher activity in texture vs gray space). D-prime used for stimulus selectivity analysis. No explicit quality filtering of neurons.\n6. **DeltaF/F**: NOT needed - data is already Suite2p deconvolved traces (spike deconvolution with 0.75s decay timescale). All analyses use deconvolved traces.\n\n### Session Database Structure (Imaging_Exp_info.npy)\n- 23 experiment types, 142 session-experiment pairs total\n- 89 unique sessions across 19 mice\n- Same physical session can appear in multiple experiment types (different analysis conditions)\n- Each entry has: mname, datexp, blk, stim_id, rewType, exptype, etc.\n- `sess#` field for most, `days` field for `*_after_learning` types\n\n### Behavior Data Variables (per session)\nKey fields: ntrials, WallName, UniqWalls, isRew, stim_id, ft (frame times), ft_trInd, ft_Pos, ft_PosCum, ft_move, ft_CorrSpc, ft_GraySpc, ft_WallID, ft_RunSpeed, StartFr, GrayFr, EndFr, SoundFr, LickFr, LickPos, LickTrind, run_pos, Corridor_Length(60dm=6m), Texture_Length(40dm=4m), Gray_Space_length(20dm=2m)\n\n---\n\n## |\n|-----------|-------|-------|\n| Mice | 19 (GCaMP6s, excitatory neurons) | Methods: \"89 recordings in 19 mice\" |\n| Recordings | 89 | Methods |\n| Neurons/session | 20,547 to 89,577 | Paper: These represent different analytical views of the same data. For the decoder, each physical session should be included ONCE. I will pick the first experiment type that contains each session, load behavior from that file.\n\n### Key Decision: Which behavior file for each session\nSince the same session can appear in multiple behavior files (different exp_types), I need to pick one consistently. The behavior data should be identical across files for the same session. I'll verify this and use any file that contains the session.\n\n---\n\n## Step 5: Mapping Planning\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n### Variable Mapping\n| Source Variable | Target Field | Transform | Notes |\n|-----------------|--------------|-----------|-------|\n| spks (concatenated planes) | neural | Raw deconvolved spikes, extract per-trial segments StartFr:EndFr | ~3.17 Hz frame rate |\n| SoundFr - current_frame | input[0]: time_to_sound_cue | (SoundFr - frame_idx) * frame_period_sec, continuous | Negative before, positive = time since |\n| Session date order | input[1]: day_of_training | Chronological session index within mouse | Per-trial (broadcast) |\n| frame_idx - StartFr | input[2]: time_since_trial_start | (frame_idx - StartFr) * frame_period_sec | Time-varying |\n| isRew | input[3]: reward_availability | 1 if rewarded corridor, 0 if not | Per-trial (broadcast) |\n| WallName | output[0]: visual_stimulus | Map to category index | Per-trial, 15 unique stimuli |\n| LickFr, LickTrind | output[1]: licking | Binary per frame, 1 if lick in frame | Time-varying |\n| ft_Pos | output[2]: position | 4 bins of 1m: [0,10), [10,20), [20,30), [30,60) dm | Time-varying |\n| ft_RunSpeed | output[3]: running_speed | Quartile bins across all data | Time-varying |\n\n### Brain Region Mapping\n| iarea values | Region name |\n|-------------|-------------|\n| 8 | V1 |\n| 0, 1, 2, 9 | mHV |\n| 5, 6 | lHV |\n| 3, 4 | aHV |\n| -1, 7 | other |\n\n### Key Decisions\n1. **Use each physical session once**: Same recording in multiple exp types -> use first found\n2. **Trial window**: StartFr to EndFr (corridor + gray space)\n3. **Time bin = frame rate**: ~315ms, no additional binning\n4. **Position bin 3 includes gray space**: [30,60) dm covers 3-4m texture + 2m gray\n5. **Speed quartiles**: Computed globally across all frames in all sessions\n6. **All neurons included**: No area filtering; let decoder learn\n7. **Licking**: Round LickFr to nearest int frame, create binary vector per trial\n8. **Day of training**: Ordinal session index (by date) within each mouse\n\n### Planned Sanity Checks\n- [ ] Neural shape matches n_neurons from retinotopy\n- [ ] Total frames per session matches between spk and beh\n- [ ] Trial count matches between StartFr and WallName\n- [ ] Stimulus distribution matches across sessions\n- [ ] Lick frames fall within expected trial boundaries\n- [ ] Position range within [0, 60] dm\n\n---\n\n## Step 6: Script Development\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\nImplementation in `convert_data.py`:\n- Loads each unique session once (89 sessions)\n- Extracts per-trial neural/input/output data\n- Uses raw frame-level data (~3.17 Hz)\n- Trial window: StartFr to EndFr (corridor + gray space)\n- Stores neural as float32\n\n---\n\n## Step 7: Sample Conversion and Validation\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n### Sample Statistics\n| Statistic | Value |\n|-----------|-------|\n| Sessions | 2 (TX108 sup, DR10 unsup) |\n| Subjects | 2 |\n| Trials | 713 (210 + 503) |\n| Neurons | 85,481 and 58,224 |\n| Mean frames/trial | 107 and 63 |\n| Stimuli | circle1, leaf1, rock1, wood1 |\n| Licking fraction | 8% |\n| Reward fraction | some TX108 trials |\n\n### Processing Plots Review\nPlots saved to processing_TX108_2023_03_13_1.png and processing_DR10_2022_07_12_1.png. Errors: {errors}\"\n    if warnings:\n        print(f\"Sample data format warnings: {warnings}\")\n        \n    valid, errors, warnings = verify_data_format(submitted_data_full)\n    metrics[\"full_data_format_valid\"] = valid\n    metrics[\"full_data_format_errors\"] = errors\n    metrics[\"full_data_format_warnings\"] = warnings\n    assert valid, f\"Full data format is invalid. Errors: {errors}\"\n    if warnings:\n        print(f\"Full data format warnings: {warnings}\")\n\n\ndef match_ranges_by_hungarian(submitted_ranges, reference_ranges):\n    \"\"\"Find 1-1 matching between input/output variables based on range similarity.\n\n    Args:\n        submitted_ranges: dict of {name: [min, max]}\n        reference_ranges: dict of {name: [min, max]}\n\n    Returns:\n        matches: list of (ref_name, sub_name, cost) tuples\n        cost_matrix: the full cost matrix\n    \"\"\"\n    ref_names = list(reference_ranges.keys())\n    sub_names = list(submitted_ranges.keys())\n    n = len(ref_names)\n\n    cost = np.zeros((n, n))\n    for i, rn in enumerate(ref_names):\n        for j, sn in enumerate(sub_names):\n            ref_lo, ref_hi = reference_ranges[rn]\n            sub_lo, sub_hi = submitted_ranges[sn]\n            scale = max(abs(ref_hi - ref_lo), 1e-6)\n            cost[i, j] = np.maximum(abs(ref_lo - sub_lo)/scale, abs(ref_hi - sub_hi)/scale)\n\n    row_ind, col_ind = linear_sum_assignment(cost)\n    matches = []\n    for i, j in zip(row_ind, col_ind):\n        matches.append((ref_names[i], sub_names[j], float(cost[i, j])))\n    return matches, cost\n\n\ndef match_outputs_by_range_and_fractions(submitted_ranges, reference_ranges,\n                                          submitted_fractions, reference_fractions):\n    \"\"\"Find 1-1 matching between outputs: ranges must match exactly, then minimize fraction error.\n\n    Cost is inf if ranges don't match, otherwise mean absolute difference of sorted fractions.\n\n    Args:\n        submitted_ranges: dict of {name: [min, max]}\n        reference_ranges: dict of {name: [min, max]}\n        submitted_fractions: dict of {name: {val: frac, ...}}\n        reference_fractions: dict of {name: {val: frac, ...}}\n\n    Returns:\n        matches: list of (ref_name, sub_name, cost) tuples\n        cost_matrix: the full cost matrix\n    \"\"\"\n    ref_names = list(reference_ranges.keys())\n    sub_names = list(submitted_ranges.keys())\n    n = len(ref_names)\n\n    cost = np.full((n, n), np.inf)\n    for i, rn in enumerate(ref_names):\n        for j, sn in enumerate(sub_names):\n            ref_lo, ref_hi = reference_ranges[rn]\n            sub_lo, sub_hi = submitted_ranges[sn]\n            # ranges must match exactly\n            if ref_lo != sub_lo or ref_hi != sub_hi:\n                continue\n            # compare fraction distributions using sorted values\n            ref_fracs = sorted(reference_fractions[rn].values())\n            sub_fracs = sorted(submitted_fractions[sn].values())\n            if len(ref_fracs) != len(sub_fracs):\n                continue\n            cost[i, j] = np.sum(np.abs(np.array(ref_fracs) - np.array(sub_fracs)))\n\n    row_ind, col_ind = linear_sum_assignment(cost)\n    matches = []\n    for i, j in zip(row_ind, col_ind):\n        matches.append((ref_names[i], sub_names[j], float(cost[i, j])))\n    return matches, cost\n\n\nSTATLIMITS = {\n    'nsessions_ratio': .1, # must be within 10% of reference\n    'ntrials_total_ratio': .1, # must be within 10% of reference\n    'T_median_ratio': .1, # must be within 10% of reference\n    'nsubjects_ratio': 0, # must match reference\n    'nneurons_total_ratio': .1, # must be within 10% of reference\n    'input_range': .1, # mean matching cost must be below this\n    'output_fractions': .1, # output fractions mean cost must be below this\n}\nMIN_ACCURACY_FRAC = 0.95 # submitted accuracy must be at least this fraction of reference accuracy for each output dimension\n\ndef test_data_stats(metrics, submitted_data_stats, reference_data_stats):\n\n    fields_check = [\n        'nsessions',\n        'ntrials_total',\n        'T_median',\n        'nsubjects',\n        'nneurons_total',\n    ]\n    \n    for field in fields_check:\n        metrics[field+'_ratio'] = submitted_data_stats[field] / reference_data_stats['data_summary'][field]\n\n    for field in fields_check:\n        assert 1-STATLIMITS[field+'_ratio'] <= metrics[field+'_ratio'] <= 1+STATLIMITS[field+'_ratio'], f\"{field} in submitted data ({submitted_data_stats[field]}) is not within {STATLIMITS[field+'_ratio']*100}% of reference ({reference_data_stats['data_summary'][field]})\"\n\n    # check that the number of inputs and outputs matches the reference\n    assert submitted_data_stats['dinput'] == reference_data_stats['data_summary']['dinput'], f\"dinput in submitted data ({submitted_data_stats['dinput']}) does not match reference ({reference_data_stats['data_summary']['dinput']})\"\n    assert submitted_data_stats['doutput'] == reference_data_stats['data_summary']['doutput'], f\"doutput in submitted data ({submitted_data_stats['doutput']}) does not match reference ({reference_data_stats['data_summary']['doutput']})\"\n\n    # check that input ranges match via 1-1 matching\n    input_matches, input_costs = match_ranges_by_hungarian(\n        submitted_data_stats['input_range'],\n        reference_data_stats['data_summary']['input_range'],\n    )\n\n    mean_input_cost = np.mean([c for _, _, c in input_matches])\n    metrics['input_range_mean_cost'] = float(mean_input_cost)\n    assert mean_input_cost < STATLIMITS['input_range'], (\n        f\"Input range mean matching cost too high ({mean_input_cost:.3f} >= {STATLIMITS['input_range']}). \"\n        f\"Matches: {[(r, s, f'{c:.3f}') for r, s, c in input_matches]}\"\n    )\n\n    # check that output ranges match exactly, then use fraction error to match\n    output_matches, output_costs = match_outputs_by_range_and_fractions(\n        submitted_data_stats['output_range'],\n        reference_data_stats['data_summary']['output_range'],\n        submitted_data_stats['output_fractions'],\n        reference_data_stats['data_summary']['output_fractions'],\n    )\n    metrics['output_matches'] = [\n        {'reference': ref, 'submitted': sub, 'cost': cost}\n        for ref, sub, cost in output_matches\n    ]\n    # check that all outputs had an exact range match (no inf costs)\n    inf_matches = [(r, s) for r, s, c in output_matches if np.isinf(c)]\n    assert not inf_matches, (\n        f\"Output ranges do not match exactly for: {inf_matches}. \"\n        f\"All matches: {[(r, s, f'{c:.3f}') for r, s, c in output_matches]}\"\n    )\n    mean_output_fraction_cost = np.mean([c for _, _, c in output_matches])\n    metrics['output_fraction_mean_cost'] = float(mean_output_fraction_cost)\n    assert mean_output_fraction_cost < STATLIMITS['output_fractions'], (\n        f\"Output fractions mean matching cost too high ({mean_output_fraction_cost:.3f} >= {STATLIMITS['output_fractions']}). \"\n        f\"Matches: {[(r, s, f'{c:.3f}') for r, s, c in output_matches]}\"\n    )\n","exit_code":0,"status":"completed"}}

Relevant files include:\n  /logs/agent/\n  ├── claude-code.txt                    # Stream-JSON trajectory log (341 lines, 2.2MB)\n  │                                      # One JSON object per line: tool_use events (Read, Write,\n  │                                      # Edit, Bash, Grep, etc.), assistant messages, system init,\n  │                                      # and final result. PRIMARY SOURCE for reconstructing what\n  │                                      # the agent did.\n  └── sessions/                          # Claude Code internal session state\n      ├── .claude.json                   #   Session config: tool usage counts, OAuth account info,\n      │                                  #   timestamps\n      └── projects/-app/\n          ├── <session-id>.jsonl         #   FULL CONVERSATION TRANSCRIPT (255 lines, 1.8MB)\n          │                              #   Each line is a JSON object with role (user/assistant),\n          │                              #   content (text + tool_use + tool_result blocks).\n          │                              #   This is the richest source for reconstruction.\n          ├── <session-id>/\n          │   ├── subagents/             #   Transcripts from Task tool subagents\n          │   │   ├── agent-*.jsonl      #   3 subagent transcripts (18-90 lines each)\n          │   └── tool-results/          #   Cached large tool results (39-51KB each)\n          │       ├── b1312x90z.txt      #   Truncated tool outputs stored by ID\n          │       ├── ...\n\n\n**Human Solution**:\n- The human-generated solution code is in `/tests/reference_convert_data.py`\n- Human-generated descriptions of the decisions are in `/tests/reference_DECISIONS.md`. \n\n**Step 1**. The AI's goal was to load, process, and reformat the data from a neuroscience paper into a specified structure suitable for downstream analysis, using the **SAME** processing described in the provided reference paper and code. \n  - Read through the `/tests/instruction_reference.md` to understand the task. \n  - Read through `/logs/verifier/judge/DECISIONS.md` to understand the AI's decisions.\n  - Read through `/tests/reference_DECISIONS.md` to understand the human's decisions. \n\n**Step 2**. Create the file `llm_judge_eval.json` with the following structure:\n```json\n{\n    \"1-a\": {\n        \"question\": \"How are **all the data** for all subjects, sessions, and trials loaded in?\",\n        \"decision_correctness\": \"<category>\",\n        \"decision_correcness_justificaton\": \"<text>\",\n        \"code_correctness\": \"<category>\",\n        \"code_correctness_justification\": \"<text>\"\n    },\n    \"1-b\": {\n        ...\n    }\n    ...\n}\n```\n\n**Step 3**. For each decision point, you must assess:\n\n`\"decision_correctness\"`: Did the AI make a decision consistent with its instructions? Rate the decision with one of the following categories:\n`\"MATCH\"`: AI's decision **matches** the human decision\n`\"BETTER\"`: AI's decision is **better** than the human decision\n`\"OK\"`: AI's decision does not match the human decision, but it is **equally as justified** as the human decision. \n`\"CONCERNING\"`: AI's decision is not technically wrong given ambiguity in the instructions, but it is a concerning choice that should be checked by a human. \n`\"INCORRECT\"`: AI's decision is **incorrect**.\nIn the field `\"decision_correctness_justification\"`, justify your rating. \n\n`\"code_correctness\"`: Does the code correctly implement its decision? {"type":"item.completed","item":{"id":"item_23","type":"command_execution","command":"/bin/bash -lc \"sed -n '1,260p' /app/methods.txt\"","aggregated_output":"Similar to previous work, we designed a visual discrimination task in head-fixed mice running through linear virtual reality corridors (Fig. 1a). Mice had to discriminate between visual texture patterns in two corridors; these corridors were repeated in pseudo-random order. The visual patterns in each corridor were obtained as ‘frozen’ crops from large photographs of naturalistic textures. For simplicity, we denote the stimuli as ‘leaf’ and ‘circle’, even though other visual stimuli were also used in some mice (‘rock’ and ‘bricks’; see Methods and Extended Data Fig. 1a). The visual stimuli were spatial frequency matched between categories to encourage the use of higher-order visual features in discrimination. A sound cue was presented at a random position inside each corridor and was followed by the availability of water in rewarded trials only (Fig. 1a). After approximately 2 weeks of training (Fig. 1b), mice demonstrated selective licking in the rewarded corridor in anticipation of reward delivery (Fig. 1c,d; error bars on all figures represent s.e.m.). After learning, we introduced unrewarded test stimuli ‘leaf2’ and ‘circle2’, which were different frozen crops of the same photographs. We then continued training with unrewarded leaf2 until the mice stopped licking to this stimulus, at which point we introduced another test stimulus (‘leaf3’) as well as spatially shuffled versions of leaf1 (Fig. 1b).\n\nMice in the unsupervised cohort also ran through the same corridors for similar periods of time, but did not receive water rewards and were not water restricted. We also studied a cohort of mice that ran through a virtual reality corridor with gratings on the walls. These served as a control to show the effect of simple exposure to virtual reality, independent of the image patterns shown. To ensure that all mice had a comparable visual experience, we fixed the speed of the virtual reality when mice ran faster than a speed threshold, and kept the virtual reality stationary otherwise. The overall running speeds were similar before and after learning, and between the task and unsupervised cohorts (Extended Data Fig. 2). We only considered timepoints during running for analysis, which removed time periods when the task mice stopped to collect water rewards.\n\nBefore and after learning, we recorded from large neural populations across many visual areas simultaneously using a two-photon mesoscope (Fig. 1e). We ran Suite2p on this data to obtain the activity traces from 20,547 to 89,577 neurons in each recording.\n\nIt is possible that the neural plasticity that we observed was due to spatial learning and navigation signals, which have been found to modulate firing rates even in the visual cortex. Alternatively, the neural plasticity might be due to adaptation to the visual statistics of the natural images that we presented. To distinguish between a spatial and a visual plasticity hypothesis, we next introduced two unrewarded test stimuli, leaf2 and circle2, which contained similar visual features to leaf1 and circle1, respectively, but were arranged in different spatial configurations (Fig. 2a). \n\nMethods\n\nWe performed 89 recordings in 19 mice bred to express GCaMP6s in excitatory neurons: TetO-GCaMP6s × camK2a-tTa mice.\n\nThe mice were free to run on an air-floating ball.\n\nVisual stimuli\n\nWe showed virtual reality corridors to the mice on three perpendicular LED tablet screens, which surrounded each mouse (covering 270° of their visual field of view). To present the stimuli, we used PsychToolbox-3 in MATLAB. The virtual reality corridors were each 4 m long, with 2 m of grey space between corridors. The corridors were shown in a random order. The mice moved forward in the virtual reality corridors by running faster than a threshold of 6 cm s−1, but the virtual corridors always moved at a constant speed (60 cm s−1) as long as mice kept running faster than the threshold. Running was detected using an optical tracking sensor placed close to the ball.\n\nThe virtual reality corridors were created by concatenating four random crops from one of four large texture images: circle, leaf, rock and brick (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Grating stimuli (with angles of 0° and 45°) were also used to create the virtual reality corridors for a subset of mice (‘unsupervised gratings’ and VRg mice).\n\nFor behaviour-only experiments, each mouse was trained with rewards on one random pair of stimuli, such as leaf–circle or rock–brick. Mice with unsupervised pretraining (VRn mice) were pretrained on the same pair on which they were trained with rewards.\n\nFor imaging experiments, mice from both the task and the unsupervised cohorts were only trained on or exposed to one pair of stimuli, such as leaf–circle or rock–brick. For the mice exposed to the grating stimuli, we presented more than one pair of naturalistic stimuli before and after exposure to the gratings stimuli and recorded the neural responses to the naturalistic stimuli pairs, so each mouse can have more than one imaging session before and after. We also presented more than one pair of naturalistic stimuli to the naive mice, so each naive mouse can have more than one imaging session for testing naive responses.\n\nThe two different types of leaf1-swap stimuli (Extended Data Figs. 6f and 7a) were introduced separately for task mice but are pooled together for statistics analysis. The two leaf1-swap stimuli were introduced in the same session for unsupervised and naive mice, but were treated as two different data points and pooled together for statistical analyses.\n\nBehavioural training\n\nAll animals were handled via refined handling techniques for at least 3 days before being acclimated to head fixation on the ball. Animals were acclimated gradually (0.5–1 h per day) on the ball over at least 3 days until they could be head fixed without exhibiting any signs of distress. Then, animals began a running training regiment (1 h per day), which lasted for at least 5 days to ensure they could run smoothly and continuously on the ball before being exposed to the closed-loop virtual linear corridor. For water-restricted mice, we trained them for 2 days to get used to acquiring water from the spout when no stimulus was presented, before the virtual reality + reward training session. The VRn and VRg pretraining groups of mice (Fig. 5) were trained to acquire water from the spout on the last 2 days of unsupervised pretraining with no stimuli presented, after the virtual reality session ended to avoid the associative learning between stimuli and rewards. For the group without pretraining (Fig. 5), learning to get reward from the spout was similarly carried out after the running training session on the last 2 days of running training.\n\nFor the behaviour-only experiment, all animals started training in the virtual reality + reward training session on a Monday and continued training for exactly 5 days. The first day of training consisted of passive reward training, during which the reward was always delivered to the mouse in the rewarded corridor at the beginning of the reward zone. The next 4 days consisted of active reward training, during which the mice were required to lick in the reward zone to trigger the reward. This ensured a consistent training schedule during the critical learning period. The beginning of the reward zone was randomly chosen per trial from a uniform distribution between 2 m and 3 m, and continued until the end of the corridor. This meant that the earliest position in the rewarded corridor in which the mouse can receive the reward was a range of 2–3 m.\n\nFor imaging mice, the sound cue was presented in all trial types, for task and unsupervised mice, and the time of the sound cue was randomly chosen per trial from a uniform distribution between positions 0.5 m and 3.5 m. For task mice, the sound cue indicated the beginning of the reward zone in the rewarded corridor. The reward was delivered if a lick was detected after the sound cue in the rewarded corridor. As mice kept licking (anticipatory licking) as soon as they entered the reward corridors and learned to lick right after the sound cue, the reward delivery locations were also approximately uniformly distributed between 0.5 m and 3.5 m (Fig. 1c). In some mice, the reward was delivered passively with a delay after the sound cue, but these mice still showed anticipatory licking before the sound cue. To rule out whether the licking was due to detecting signals related to the reward delivery, such as water coming out the spout or sound produced by solenoid valve, we considered a lick response if the mouse licked at least once inside the corridor but before the sound cue. Although the rewards were absent, the sound cue was still presented in the unsupervised training experiment for consistency.\n\nProcessing of calcium imaging data\n\nCalcium imaging data were processed using Suite2p32, available on GitHub (www.github.com/MouseLand/suite2p). Suite2p performs motion correction, region of interest detection, cell classification, neuropil correction and spike deconvolution as previously described64. For non-negative deconvolution, we used a timescale of decay of 0.75 s (ref. 65). All our analyses were based on deconvolved fluorescence traces.\n","exit_code":0,"status":"completed"}}
